question: A small GQA transformer (226M params) was trained at context 1024 on a 6GB GPU. What are the most practical ways to make it effectively handle 4k-32k context: RoPE/YaRN fine-tuning, sliding-window attention, context compression into soft tokens (ICAE/gisting), memory modules (RMT, Infini-attention, Titans), KV-cache tricks? Rank by feasibility and cost.
answer:
To scale your 226M parameter GQA transformer from 1k to 4k–32k context on a 6GB GPU, prioritize techniques by their impact on memory and implementation feasibility.

1. KV Cache Quantization (High Feasibility): Compressing the KV cache to INT8 or INT4 is the most practical way to reduce memory usage by 50–75% with minimal quality degradation [1]. This is standard for production and highly effective.

2. PagedAttention (High Feasibility): Use vLLM or similar frameworks to implement PagedAttention. It eliminates memory fragmentation and improves memory efficiency by 60–80%, allowing for larger batch sizes or longer contexts within the same 6GB limit [1].

3. RoPE Scaling (Moderate Feasibility): To prevent performance collapse beyond the 1024-token training limit, apply YaRN or NTK-aware scaling during a brief continued-pretraining stage. This is necessary to keep positional encodings usable at 4k–32k lengths [2][3].

4. Sliding-Window Attention (Moderate Feasibility): This limits KV cache growth to O(window_size) rather than O(sequence_length), providing fixed memory overhead [1]. Note that it may degrade long-range retrieval accuracy [3][1].

5. Memory Modules / Compression (Low Feasibility): Techniques like ICAE or Infini-attention offer significant compression but typically require additional training (pretraining or fine-tuning) to integrate effectively [4][5]. These are more complex to deploy than inference-time cache management [6].

For a 6GB constraint, combine GQA (already present), INT8 KV cache quantization, and PagedAttention as your baseline strategy [1]. If you must exceed 32k, research implementations of Ring Attention or memory-efficient linear attention variations [1].
